question.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y={y}^{2}{e}^{x}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-1,\,q(x)={e}^{x},\,n=2.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{-1}={e}^{x}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z={e}^{x}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-{e}^{x}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=1,\,Q(x)=-{e}^{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z) & ={e}^{x}\cdot (-{e}^{x}) \\ {e}^{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z{e}^{x} & =-{e}^{2x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x}) & =-{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =-\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{x} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{2{e}^{x}}{C-{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-3{x}^{2}z={x}^{2}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-15{x}^{2}z=5{x}^{2}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-15{x}^{2},\,Q(x)=5{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-15{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-5{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=1,\,q(x)=-x,\,n=3.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3}\frac{dy}{dx}+{y}^{-2}=-x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-x
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2z=2x
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-2,\,Q(x)=2x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-2)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-2x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2z) & ={e}^{-2x}\cdot (2x) \\ {e}^{-2x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2z{e}^{-2x} & =2x{e}^{-2x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-2x}) & =2x{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-2x})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x{e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{-2x} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2x}(2x+1)+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C{e}^{2x}-2x-1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-2}=\frac{C{e}^{2x}-2x-1}{2}\,⇒\,y=\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{C{e}^{2x}-2x-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.

In this case, we have

$$

$$
{y}^{-1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{1/2}=1.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-1/2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z=1
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2}z=\frac{1}{2}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-\frac{1}{2},\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-1/2)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-x/2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x/2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2}z) & ={e}^{-x/2}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}) \\ {e}^{-x/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2}z{e}^{-x/2} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x/2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-x/2}) & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

$$
p(x)=-\frac{1}{x},\,q(x)=\sqrt{x},\,n=2.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{x}{y}^{-1}=\sqrt{x}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z=\sqrt{x}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=-\sqrt{x}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-\sqrt{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-\sqrt{x}) \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-x\sqrt{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =-{x}^{3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =\int -{x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =-\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-2{x}^{5/2}}{5x},\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-2{x}^{5/2}}{5x}\,⇒\,y=\frac{5x}{C-2{x}^{5/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y={x}^{2}{y}^{3/4}.

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y={x}^{2}{y}^{3/4} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{y}{x} & =x{y}^{3/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={x}^{-1},\,q(x)=x,\,n=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3/4},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3/4}\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{-1}{y}^{1/4}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/4}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}{y}^{-3/4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3/4}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
4\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{-1}z=x
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-1}z=\frac{x}{4}
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{4x},\,Q(x)=\frac{x}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/4x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{(1/4)\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{1/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{1/4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{1/4}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-1}z) & ={x}^{1/4}\cdot (\frac{x}{4}) \\ {x}^{1/4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/4}z & =\frac{{x}^{5/4}}{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{1/4}) & =\frac{{x}^{5/4}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{1/4})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{x}^{5/4}}{4}\,\text{d}x \\ z{x}^{1/4} & =\frac{1}{9}{x}^{9/4}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{9/4}+C}{9{x}^{1/4}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=9{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{1/4}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{1/4}=\frac{{x}^{9/4}+C}{9{x}^{1/4}}\,⇒\,y={(\frac{{x}^{9/4}+C}{9{x}^{1/4}})}^{4}\,.

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2{x}^{-1}z={x}^{-2}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}-xy.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{-1/2}-xy \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+xy & ={y}^{-1/2} \\ \frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{-1}y & ={x}^{-2}{y}^{-1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={x}^{-1},\,q(x)={x}^{-2},\,n=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we multiply the differential equation by ${y}^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{-1}{y}^{3/2}={x}^{-2}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{3/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{2}{y}^{1/2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{-1}z={x}^{-2}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-1}z=\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-2}
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{3}{2x},\,Q(x)=\frac{3}{2{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/2x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{(3/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{3/2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3/2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-1}z) & ={x}^{3/2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-2}) \\ {x}^{3/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{1/2}z & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2}z) & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{2}{x}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{3/2}z & =3{x}^{1/2}+C \\ z & =\frac{3\sqrt{x}+C}{{x}^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{3/2}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{3/2}=\frac{3\sqrt{x}+C}{{x}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{{(3\sqrt{x}+C)}^{2/3}}{x}\,.
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy & ={x}^{3}{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{x} & =x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-\frac{1}{x},\,q(x)=x,\,n=2.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{{y}^{-1}}{x}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z=x
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=-x
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-x) \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
